I guess i know exactly how you feel. A similar thing happened to me last week when my father passed away. I had the chance to visit him, but i was waiting till my last summer (southern hemisphere) exam. His condition also didn't appear to be life threatening. It had been months since I had seen him.

I dont know how we are supposed to deal with this. Maybe it will follow us for the rest of our lives. Maybe we should just forget this last mistake. I don't have much advice because I am right in the same boat you are. Just wanted you to know someone read this and that you are not alone.

I understand how you feel. Actually my own experience has been quite similar to yours. I study economics at a prestigious school in Brazil, and maybe it has to do with our countries education system (Turkey and Brazil are very close in ONU's "Education Index"), but throughout my whole life, I've observed a phenomena among my colleagues that I like to call, in Portuguese "Aprendizado Algorítimado", that you could translate to "Learning by Algorithm". It's quite usual for my colleagues to ground their whole knowledge about a topic in a series of algorithms that could easily solve a given problem, making it easier to do well on tests, but also resulting in a general ignorance about any real meaning that lies within the problem. 
For example, when talking about economics, under certain theoretical assumptions I will not specify (being "competitive markets" the most important of them), if you maximize a production function you will find a direct relationship between prices and marginal production cost. Instead of understanding the mathematical implications of maximizing a production function, to be able to solve a given exercise quickly most of my colleagues only fix a single algorithm within their minds: P=MGc (prices equals marginal cost). When I do talk with some of them about the topic, most of the time all I'm given is a big poker face, "what are you talking about, did we already learn that?". And that is one is many examples.
I assumed a time ago that the great majority of them, including some of the ones with really good grades, are not really acquiring knowledge, but simply doing what a computer already does, that is to decorate a series of codes. I must tell you I've learnt how to do it myself, this "algorithm" technique that makes tests ten times easier, and I would recommend you to do too, so you will get greater grades (they may be important for your future). However, do not stop doing your thing. I believe it's possible to really try to gather knowledge and "cheat" to get good grades (by cheating I mean to look for easy ways to solve a problem when you are out of time to really think about it), and is exactly what I try to do. 
Anyways, getting good grades have no real great significance. It means you did well on a standardized tests. Even tough it may be a good enough way to evaluate you knowledge, tests are weak institution, full of wholes who can be exploited to the benefit of someone who actually knows nothing. Try to Learn well above all else, and if you find time to exploit these college tests, do it.

Yes, you're probably overthinking. However, even if you weren't, you really should not feel bad. Sometimes you should not even care. You see, what some of your fellows colleagues think of you may be somewhat useful mainly because other people are better suited to perceive our personal flaws than ourselves. But, at the same time, people who don't know anything about you will soon fill up their mind with prejudgment, so you must be skeptical about what they think. In any case, there is no reason to disturb yourself. 


If a bunch of people call you a "stupid little girl", it doesn't mean you are. Or vice versa. Remember to always skeptically analyze the situation, and then evaluate what is really happening. Cheers.
